chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-01.title: Find $f$ explicitly
chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-01.body:
If $x=\sqrt5+\sqrt2$ then $x^2=7+2\sqrt{10}$, so $(x^2-7)^2=40$. Hence $g(x)=(x^2-7)^2-40=x^4-14x^2+9$ is a monic rational polynomial with root $\sqrt5+\sqrt2$. It is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (its roots $\pm\sqrt5\pm\sqrt2$ are irrational, and none satisfies a rational quadratic), so $f=g$ because a monic irreducible polynomial with a given root is its minimal polynomial. Also $g(\sqrt5-\sqrt2)=0$ (it is another root). Therefore $f(f(\sqrt5-\sqrt2))=f(0)=(0-7)^2-40=9$.

**Answer: 9**

chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-02.title: Power of a point three times
chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-02.body:
As in the figure, the chord $EF$ lies along line $AB$ (order $E,A,B,F$), chord $GH$ along $BC$ (order $G,B,C,H$) and chord $IJ$ along $CA$ (order $J,A,C,I$). Let $e=AE$, $g=BG$, $i=CI$. Then $AF=12-e$, $BE=6+e$, $BF=6-e$; $BH=15-g$, $CG=7+g$, $CH=8-g$; $AI=9+i$, $AJ=7-i$, $CJ=16-i$. Power of a point at $A$, $B$, $C$:
$$e(12-e)=(9+i)(7-i),\quad g(15-g)=(6+e)(6-e),\quad i(16-i)=(7+g)(8-g).$$
Adding, $12e+15g+16i-e^2-g^2-i^2=155-2i+g-e^2-g^2-i^2$, so $12e+14g+18i=155$, i.e. $6e+7g+9i=\frac{155}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{155}{2}$**

chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-03.title: Reduce to a $1\times10$ strip
chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-03.body:
Call the tiles the $\Gamma$-tile (three cells: top row of two, plus the cell below the left one), the I-tile (a vertical domino) and the J-tile (three cells: bottom row of two plus the cell above the right one). Each $\Gamma$-tile must be paired with a J-tile to form a $2\times3$ rectangle (nothing else can fill the cell next to a $\Gamma$-tile's hole), and I-tiles are $2\times1$ rectangles. So we tile a $2\times10$ grid with $2\times3$ and $2\times1$ rectangles, equivalent to tiling a $1\times10$ strip with $1\times3$ and $1\times1$ pieces. With $T_n=T_{n-1}+T_{n-3}$ and $T_0=T_1=T_2=1$: $1,1,1,2,3,4,6,9,13,19,28$. So $T_{10}=28$. (An exhaustive search over the three tiles gives $28$ too.)

**Answer: 28**

chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-04.title: Prime factorization
chmmc-2010-winter-tiebreaker-04.body:
$2010=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot67$ is a product of four distinct primes, so it has $2^4=16$ positive divisors.

**Answer: 16**
